newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus judge accuses Lukashenko of vandalism.
newsitem.headline: Belarus judge accuses Lukashenko of vandalism.

text.p: The head of the highest court in Belarus announced his resignation on Wednesday and accused President Alexander Lukashenko of trampling on the rule of law, destroying democracy and setting up a dictatorship.
Valery Tikhinya said he, his deputy and two other judges had resigned from the former Soviet republic's constitutional court, and the remaining seven judges could follow suit before long.
He blamed Lukashenko for pressing ahead with a referendum which his court opposed and has been denounced by the West.
"An act of legal vandalism has occurred. I cannot carry out my duties in these circumstances," he told a news conference.

Lukashenko, 42, used a landslide victory in the November 24 poll to rewrite the constitution, awarding himself significant powers over rival branches of power -- including the right to appoint half the court judges and sack its chairman.
He warned the judges after the referendum that they would only keep their jobs if they gave up their "political bias".
Lukashenko had ignored rulings by Tikhinya's court which ruled 19 of his decrees were anti-constitutional.

"A dictatorship of one individual was set up when the new, illegitimate constitution was approved," Tikhinya said. "The principle of democracy has been destroyed...There is the power of law and the law of power. The law of power has won."
Tikhinya's deputy Valery Fadeyev, and two other judges, Mikhail Pastukhov and Alexander Vashkevich, also resigned.
"I do not think that will be the end of the resignations. These are just the ones I know about for now," Tikhinya said.

But Lukashenko has weathered a storm of criticism and resignations -- including that of his prime minister days before the vote -- and he has the backing of a new lower house of parliament called by him after the referendum.
The new, smaller chamber is filled with his supporters, leaving a minority of opposition deputies, including parliament speaker Semyon Sharetsky, powerless to influence events.
The hardline leader shrugged off a public rebuke at a summit of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) which ended in Lisbon on Tuesday.
He told Europe's top security body not to meddle after it said the vote contradicted constitutional procedures and could not be considered as legitimate.

The OSCE, echoing comments by the Council of Europe and the U.S. State Department, urged Lukashenko to ensure the freedom of the media, re-establish full democratic procedures and start talking to the opposition.
Tikhinya thanked them for criticising the vote, which his court ruled should only be advisory in line with the old constitution. Lukashenko decreed it would be legally binding.
"The president's constitution must not be recognised, even if 101 percent voted for it," he said.
More than 70 percent of the electorate backed Lukashenko but serious flaws were observed in the voting which took place amid an aggressive, extremely one-sided media campaign.
The judges handed their resignations to Sharetsky in line with the old constitution, under which parliament elected them 2-1/2 years ago for 11-year terms.
